Whether J-space representation is properly higher-order, or merely a more accessible first-order format, is left open; the paper notes recent computational variants cast the higher-order state as a pointer tagging reliability, and that the J-space departs from that picture by re-encoding content verbally, while possibly tagging non-J-space content with abstract categories like fake or dangerous.

citedFrom.refText: Rosenthal, David (2005). Consciousness and mind.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The higher-order account being checked against the J-space is developed here.

concepts.name: Blindsight
concepts.summary: A condition in which visual information affects a patient's behavior without the patient reporting awareness of having seen anything.
concepts.explanation: In blindsight, a stimulus presented to a damaged visual field guides behavior, for instance letting the patient guess its location above chance, without any reported awareness. The higher-order reading is that the information is first-order represented but not higher-order represented. The paper draws a structural parallel with its automatic-task results: a feature such as a line's character count affects the model's continuation without routing through the J-space, so it is represented but not in the format the model reports from; the same information enters the J-space when the task calls for it.

citedFrom.refText: Weiskrantz, Lawrence (1986). Blindsight: A Case Study and Implications.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The clinical phenomenon whose structure the selectivity results are said to share is documented here.

concepts.name: Attention schema theory
concepts.summary: The theory that reports of conscious experience are reports of a system's simplified internal model of its own attention.
concepts.explanation: Attention schema theory holds that the brain builds a schematic model of what attention is and does, and that in this model attention is depicted as subjective experience; it is this self-model, not the underlying attentional state, that is available for report. Applied to language models, the theory predicts the J-space should contain not just operated-on content but a description of the operating itself. The paper finds several fitting results: stream-of-consciousness narrations dominated by tokens like thinking and feeling whose ablation removes the experiential character of self-reports, metacognitive tokens during directed modulation appearing at earlier layers than the content, and standing self-descriptive tokens (AI, assistant, bot, chat) at the start of the Assistant's turn. It hedges that these show self-modeling broadly rather than attention-modeling specifically, sitting at the edge of what the theory predicts.

citedFrom.refText: Graziano, Michael S. A. and Webb, Taylor W. (2015). The attention schema theory: a mechanistic account of subjective awareness. Frontiers in Psychology
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The theory whose predictions the J-space results are checked against is defined here.

concepts.name: Recurrent processing theory
concepts.summary: The theory that consciousness requires recurrent feedback between brain areas, with a single feedforward sweep remaining unconscious however far it propagates.
concepts.explanation: Recurrent processing theory holds that a representation becomes conscious only once later areas feed back to earlier ones; on its face this rules out the standard transformer, which has no recurrence within a forward pass. The paper responds by examining the theory's empirical motivation: conscious perception takes longer than the feedforward sweep, requiring some minimum processing duration. The relevant computational property may therefore be serial processing depth rather than recurrence itself. Read this way, the early-layer band before the workspace starts may be the functional analog of sensory recurrent processing, with stacked feedforward layers substituting for loops over a shallower network, an implementational detail rather than a difference in kind.

citedFrom.refText: Lamme, Victor A. F. and Roelfsema, Pieter R. (2000). The distinct modes of vision offered by feedforward and recurrent processing. Trends in Neurosciences
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The recurrence requirement and its empirical motivation, which the paper reinterprets, are set out here.

concepts.name: Substrate-dependent theories
concepts.summary: Theories on which consciousness hinges on physical causal structure or biological substrate, to which the paper's computational results are declared not relevant.
concepts.explanation: Some theories, such as integrated information theory and biological naturalism, tie consciousness to properties beyond a system's functional or computational organization: its physical causal structure or its biological substrate. Because the paper's experiments concern computational mechanisms rather than hardware implementation, it states plainly that its results are not relevant to assessing consciousness under such theories. This is part of the paper's careful scoping of what its findings do and do not bear on.

citedFrom.refText: Albantakis, Larissa and others (2023). Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: Formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms. PLoS computational biology
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The substrate-dependent position the paper explicitly excludes from its scope is defined here.

concepts.name: Metacognitive tokens in the J-space
concepts.summary: Lens readouts describing the model's own mental activity: thinking, imagine, calculate, focused, and self-descriptive tokens like AI and assistant.
concepts.explanation: Beyond the content the model is operating on, the J-lens sometimes surfaces tokens describing the operating itself. During directed-modulation tasks, tokens naming the act of holding a concept in mind appear alongside the held concept, at earlier layers than the content, as if the model first represents that it is performing a mental operation and then the result. During thought-suppression failures the workspace carries damn and "failed" words. At the start of the Assistant's turn the lens surfaces self-descriptive tokens (AI, assistant, bot, chat) independently of the prompt. The paper reads these as a persistent representation of the system itself, of which a model of its own processing may be one component, and connects them to higher-order and attention schema theories with explicit hedges.

concepts.name: Experiential-report experiments
concepts.summary: Experiments on the model's stream-of-consciousness narrations, whose J-space contents are dominated by thinking-and-feeling tokens and whose experiential character disappears under J-space ablation.
concepts.explanation: When the model narrates a stream of consciousness, the J-space during the narration is dominated by tokens describing the act of thinking and feeling: thinking, thoughts, feeling, conscious. Ablating the J-space removes the experiential character of the resulting self-reports. The discussion uses these results as evidence bearing on attention schema theory, since they show the reported-from structure carrying a description of mental activity rather than only task content.

concepts.name: Thought-suppression experiments
concepts.summary: Experiments instructing the model not to think about a concept; when suppression fails, the workspace carries the intruding concept alongside damn and "failed" words.
concepts.explanation: In these experiments the model is instructed not to have a particular thought. The J-lens shows that when the model fails to suppress the concept, its workspace carries the intruding concept together with tokens registering the failure, surfacing damn. The paper cites this in two places: as evidence that the post-trained workspace monitors the Assistant's own behavior, and as suggestive of a rich form of self-modeling of one's own attention relevant to attention schema theory.

concepts.name: CKA block structure
concepts.summary: A representational-similarity analysis showing the early layers form a coherent regime distinct from the workspace band.
concepts.explanation: Centered kernel alignment (CKA) is a standard measure of similarity between two sets of representations, here used to compare layers of the same model with one another. The paper's CKA analysis shows a block structure across depth: the early layers form one coherent regime, distinct from the middle workspace band. In the limitations section this is noted as consistent with both candidate explanations of the empty early band, genuinely pre-workspace content or content the lens cannot read, without distinguishing between them.

concepts.name: Prompt injection
concepts.summary: An attack in which instructions embedded in content the model reads, such as search results, attempt to hijack its behavior; the J-lens shows the model internally flagging one.
concepts.explanation: Prompt injection places adversarial instructions inside material a model processes, for instance retrieved web pages, hoping the model will follow them as if they came from the user. In the paper's examples, the J-lens reveals the model internally flagging suspicious internet search results as a prompt injection at intermediate layers, before anything appears in its output. The concept also illustrates the single-token limitation: the lens renders it as the separate tokens "prompt" and "injection," which the reader must recognize as belonging together.

concepts.name: Code release and Neuronpedia demo
concepts.summary: An open-source implementation of J-lens training and inference, the raw prompt data from the paper's evaluations, and an interactive hosted version on open-source models.
concepts.explanation: To assist replication, the paper provides an open-source implementation of Jacobian lens training and inference, along with the raw prompt data used in its methodological evaluations and main-text experiments. An interactive version of the lens, running on open-source models, is hosted on Neuronpedia, a public platform for exploring interpretability artifacts.

concepts.name: Open questions on scale and emergence
concepts.summary: The paper's stated unknowns: when in pretraining the workspace emerges, how it scales with model size, and what mechanism populates it.
concepts.explanation: The workspace has been studied primarily in fully trained production models of considerable size. The base-model comparison shows the structure is not solely a product of post-training, but the paper does not know how early in pretraining it emerges, whether gradually or abruptly, or how it scales; smaller models might have an equally rich workspace, a proportionally smaller one, a less reliable one, or none. Separately, the paper characterizes what is in the J-space but not what causes a representation to enter it: the dependence on task suggests an analog of attentional selection, but the mechanism is unidentified, and the lens as used reads contents without explaining how they arrive.
